info.description:
# Merged Masterclass Backend - All APIs

GENERATED from the live URLconf by `Miscellaneous/Scripts/generate_postman_collection.py` on 2026-09-21.
Do not hand-edit: re-run the script after any routing change.

**111 mounted API routes** -> **118 requests** across **15 folders**. The Django admin UI is excluded; it is not an API surface.

Request bodies: 36 of 44 write endpoints carry a template generated from the view's own validator. The rest either take no body by design (stated on the request) or use a pattern the generator does not yet read.

## Setup

1. Import all four files and select the LOCAL, UAT or PROD environment.
2. Set `login_identifier` to the e-mail or phone you are testing with.
3. Send **POST auth-otp-send-v1**, put the code you receive in `otp_code`, then send **POST auth-otp-verify-v1**.

That is the whole setup. `token` and `refresh_token` are written by the scripts - do not paste a token in by hand, and do not expect one to survive a logout.

Webhook requests are the exception: they are `noauth` and carry their own secret header, so set `lms_notification_webhook_key` and `miles_one_webhook_secret` for folder 15.

## What runs automatically

Everything below is Postman-side scripting. There is no companion runner and nothing writes to disk; the environment is the only state.

- **The access token renews itself.** The collection pre-request script reads `exp` out of the JWT and refreshes when fewer than `token_refresh_skew_seconds` (120) remain. Refresh tokens ROTATE, so the new pair is stored immediately - which is also why nothing here ever refreshes twice at once. Set `auto_refresh` to `off` to stop it.
- **Path parameters fill themselves.** After any 2xx JSON response the collection test script walks the body and writes any key matching a path variable into the environment, so a list request sets up the detail request that follows it. `id` is deliberately NOT harvested - it is the path parameter of one route (the certificate webhook) and the commonest key in every list body, so set it by hand. It fills a variable ONLY WHEN THAT VARIABLE IS EMPTY, so a value you pinned yourself is never overwritten - clear it if you want it re-harvested. Set `auto_capture` to `off` to stop it. Only the FIRST element of a list is read, and only keys named exactly like the path variable.
- **Every response is checked for the baseline**: no 5xx, and a JSON content type parses. Response time is logged, never asserted - it is a property of the machine the run is on.
- **A 401 or 403 explains itself** in the console instead of leaving a bare status code: whether a token is set at all, and whether a webhook secret rather than a token is what the route wanted.
- **The three session routes carry their own scripts** - verify stores the minted pair, refresh stores the rotated pair, logout clears both, and only on a 2xx.

Query parameters are present but DISABLED, so a request sends nothing it was not asked to send.

## What each request tells you

Open any request's Documentation pane. It carries the view and permission behind the route, the body it accepts, the query parameters it declares, every error `code` it can return and what each one means, and the shape of the response - taken from the contracts the frontend web team works to. There is no separate documentation folder to go and read: the detail is on the request you are about to send.

## Folders

- **01. Authentication and Session** - 5 routes, 5 requests (5 UNIVERSAL).
- **02. Account, Profile and Reference Content** - 9 routes, 12 requests (9 UNIVERSAL).
- **03. Masterclass - Learning Flow (app)** - 27 routes, 27 requests (26 APP, 1 WEBHOOK).
- **04. MasterclassWeb - Learning Flow (web)** - 19 routes, 19 requests (19 WEB).
- **05. AI Labs** - 5 routes, 5 requests (5 UNIVERSAL).
- **06. Events and Bookings** - 6 routes, 6 requests (2 APP, 2 UNIVERSAL, 2 WEB).
- **07. CAIRA - Badges, Certificates, CPE** - 1 routes, 1 requests (1 UNIVERSAL).
- **08. Notifications and Bell** - 5 routes, 5 requests (5 UNIVERSAL).
- **09. Catalogue** - 11 routes, 11 requests (11 UNIVERSAL).
- **10. Commerce** - 7 routes, 11 requests (7 UNIVERSAL).
- **11. Engagement - Likes, Saves, Watches** - 4 routes, 4 requests (4 UNIVERSAL).
- **12. Homepage Content** - 3 routes, 3 requests (3 UNIVERSAL).
- **13. Industry Unplugged** - 2 routes, 2 requests (2 UNIVERSAL).
- **14. Varun Masterclass** - 5 routes, 5 requests (5 UNIVERSAL).
- **15. Inbound Webhooks (secret header, no JWT)** - 2 routes, 2 requests (2 WEBHOOK).

## Conventions that apply to every request

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



## 1. Conventions

### 1.1 Every path moved under `account/`, and there is no redirect

Ported paths were namespaced under `account/` on 2026-08-12. Django does not treat `faqs` and
`account/faqs` as the same route, so an un-updated build gets a **404, not a redirect**. No shim exists.

Two legacy oddities are reproduced on purpose and are not typos to fix on your side:

- `app-maintainance` is **misspelt**, and the JSON key `app_under_maintainance` matches it. Both stay.
- Every path now carries a trailing slash, including `country` and `faqs`, which did not have one in legacy.

### 1.2 Authentication

`Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` where the table says JWT. A **bad or expired token answers `403`, not `401`** -
DRF downgrades an authentication failure when the authenticator does not implement `authenticate_header()`, and
ours does not. Do not key token-refresh on 401 alone.

The endpoints marked "enforced in handler" are a different shape: they carry no permission class, so an
anonymous request reaches the handler and gets a **401** from an explicit check inside it. So on those four you
can see 401 for anonymous and 403 for a broken token, from the same route.

### 1.3 Undeclared keys are rejected

Request bodies and query strings are validated strictly. A key the endpoint does not declare is a 400 naming
it. Sending a known key as `null` is also rejected where the field does not allow null - strict validation
forbids the key's *presence*, so "send it as null to be safe" does not work.

### 1.4 Error envelopes

The auth proxy routes (section 2) return **the SSO's own body, whole and untouched**, whatever it contains.
Everything this backend generates itself uses one of:

```json
{ "message": "Sign-in is temporarily unavailable. Please try again." }
{ "code": "account_blocked", "message": "This account has been blocked..." }
{ "message": "Invalid request.", "details": { "country": ["..."] } }
```

DRF validation failures on the serializer-backed routes come back as DRF's native shape - a map of field name
to a list of messages - not the `{status, code, errors[]}` envelope the Events routes use. **The two apps do
not share an error shape.** Handle both.

---

## 2. The login flow

Five routes, in order. All five are proxies onto the Miles SSO auth API: they OBTAIN a token, they do not
verify one. Verification is local, against the issuer's JWKS, on every subsequent request.

```
auth-identify  ->  auth-otp-send  ->  auth-otp-verify  ->  (session)
                                                             |
                                            auth-token-refresh (rotate)
                                                             |
                                                       auth-logout
```

### 8.2 The two apps do not share an error shape

Events returns `{status, code, errors[]}` and asks you to switch on `code`. Accounts returns DRF's native
validation shape, a bare `{message}`, or the SSO's body untouched. There is no single error parser that covers
both. See 1.4.

### 8.3 The auth routes return the SSO's body, not ours

Everything on the five auth routes except the two local flags and the refusals listed in 2.3 is passed through
from the Miles SSO verbatim, including fields not documented here. Treat unknown keys as additive, and do not
assume our version pins their schema.

## 1. Conventions

### 1.1 Three path prefixes, and the split is deliberate

- `api/v1/events/...` - SHARED. The registration handshake. One write path, one contract, one set of side
  effects (Zoom -> Booking -> Salesforce). A web caller and an app caller register identically.
- `web-api/v1/events/...` - WEB-ONLY READS. The landing feed and the detail page behind it.
- `app-api/v1/events/...` - APP-ONLY READS. The bookings feed.

What a page renders is genuinely surface-shaped: bucket counts, ordering and payload width differ between a
browser and a phone, so a read belongs to the surface that renders it. No route has a twin on the other read
prefix yet.

The rule this encodes: writes stay shared, reads split by surface.

`app-api/` was added on 2026-09-17 and `all-bookings/` moved onto it. An earlier version of this document
described that route as web-only; that was wrong, and the prefix is the part of this scheme that names the
surface, so it was corrected rather than left. It was MOVED, not aliased - this document went out the same
day, so there is no shipped client on the old path.

Note that `Masterclass` splits web from app a DIFFERENT way, by domain segment (`api/v1/masterclass/` vs
`api/v1/masterclass-web/`). Which scheme a surface uses is a fact to look up, not to derive.

### 1.2 Authentication

`Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` on every route above, except `webinar-main-page?login_type=pre_login`, which is
served anonymously.

**`webinar-details-page` TAKES NO `login_type` AND IS NOT GATED.** It derives the surface from the request:
send a token and you get the post-login page with its `registration` block, send none and you get the
pre-login page without it. A signed-out visitor can open a webinar page.

**CHANGED 2026-09-18.** It shipped on 2026-09-17 as `IsAuthenticated`, answering `403` to anonymous callers.
If you built against that, the 403 is gone and `data.login_type` now tells you which surface you received.

A BAD OR EXPIRED TOKEN ANSWERS `403`, NOT `401`. This is true of every authenticated route in this backend,
not just these four: DRF downgrades an authentication failure to 403 when the authenticator does not implement
`authenticate_header()`, and ours does not. Do not key token-refresh logic on 401 alone. The one `401` this app
returns is a different case entirely - see section 6.2.

### 1.3 Undeclared parameters are rejected, not ignored

Every request body and query string is validated strictly. A key the endpoint does not declare is a 400 naming
that key; it is not silently dropped. A typo'd filter therefore fails loudly instead of returning an
unfiltered 200.

### 1.4 Error envelopes

Validation failure (400):

```json
{
  "status": "error",
  "code": "invalid_request",
  "errors": [{ "field": "login_type", "message": "Field required" }]
}
```

`field` is dot-joined, so a bad key inside a list element reads as `chapters.0.chapter_id`. An undeclared key
comes back with that key as `field`.

Domain refusal (400 / 404 / 409):

```json
{ "status": "error", "code": "webinar_not_found", "detail": "Webinar does not exist." }
```

SWITCH ON `code`, NEVER ON THE HTTP STATUS AND NEVER ON `detail`. The `code` values are the stable contract;
wording and status can move.

One inconsistency to handle before you write the error handler: the `authentication_required` refusal from
`webinar-main-page` carries `message` where every other refusal carries `detail`. Read `detail ?? message`.

### 1.5 Status codes are real

The legacy V4 register endpoint answered `500` for every input and state problem, because FE reserved 400/404
for token-refresh and logout flows. These routes return the real `400` / `404` / `409` / `401`. If an
interceptor still treats any 4xx as a session problem, that has to change before you point at these routes.
A client that switches on `code` rather than on status needs no change.

### 2.1 `POST auth-identify/` - how does this person authenticate?

The first call of any login, always.

```json
{ "identifier": "learner@example.com" }
```

`identifier` is an email, phone number or username - the SSO works out which. `appCode` is **not accepted from
the client**; it is added server-side, because it names which application is asking and a caller must not be
able to claim to be another one.

The response is the SSO's, and carries `methods`, `defaultMethod`, masked destinations and `communicationId`.

**Render `methods` rather than assuming a form.** When enterprise SSO ships, this same endpoint starts
answering `saml` with a redirect. A client that renders the list needs no change; one that hardcoded an OTP box
needs a rewrite.

**Do not build a "no such account" message from this response.** An identifier the SSO has never seen returns
the same `methods`, `defaultMethod` and masks as a known one - the masks are built from what was typed, not
from anything stored. There is no negative signal here to render, by design.

This route discloses account existence through `communicationId` (null for an unknown identifier), which is why
it is **first-party only** and the most tightly throttled of the five at 20/min. Do not expose it to an
untrusted origin.

### 2.5 `POST auth-logout/` - end the session at the SSO

Empty body. Takes the bearer from the inbound `Authorization` header and forwards it.

Missing or non-Bearer header is a 401 with
`{"message": "Authorization header with a Bearer token is required."}`.

Note this deliberately does **not** resolve the token to a local user first: logout must work for a token this
database has no row for, because a session worth ending still exists.

### 2.2 `POST auth-otp-send/` - send a one-time code

```json
{ "identifier": "learner@example.com" }
```

The response carries `channel` and `cooldownSeconds`.

**Write UI copy from the returned `channel`, never from what you sent.** It is `email`, `sms` or `whatsapp`,
and phone routing is a table at the SSO that changes with no deploy on either side. **As of 2026-09-08 every
country resolves to `sms`, India included** - WhatsApp routing is off until delivery is proved end to end.

`cooldownSeconds` is how long the resend button stays disabled. Read it; do not hardcode one.

`channel` is **not accepted as an input** yet. The SSO takes it as an optional override, but this route does not
declare it, so sending it is a 400.

**A `503` means nothing was sent and nothing will be.** The identity store accepted the request and then
refused to deliver. Advance the user to a retry, never to a code-entry screen. It says our mailer is broken -
it never says anything about the account. Every identifier-specific outcome is a 200.

One caveat on phone identifiers: they are proxied faithfully rather than refused, so a **well-formed Indian
phone number can reach a silent failure** - the provider accepts the SMS and the carrier drops it, so a 200 does
not prove a message arrived. The client is currently the only thing preventing that. A *malformed* number is
not your problem: the SSO answers 400 with copy written for a learner, and that message reaches the phone field
unaltered - render it.

### 2.3 `POST auth-otp-verify/` - exchange the code for a session

```json
{ "identifier": "learner@example.com", "code": "123456" }
```

`code` is a **string, and its length is not validated here**. The code length is set server-side at the SSO -
read it rather than hardcoding six boxes.

On success the body carries `accessToken` and `refreshToken`. For a web client the SSO **also** sets the
httpOnly `miles_sso_refresh` cookie, which is forwarded verbatim.

Two **local** flags are merged into the success body, and they are the reason this route is worth reading
carefully. Neither is in the token, and the SSO knows nothing about either:

| Key | Values | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `profile_status` | `new_user`, `onboard_completed`, `profile_completed` | This platform's onboarding milestone. |
| `is_test_user` | boolean | Gates `#TestCourse` visibility. Always `false` on a fresh account - set by an admin. |

**`profile_status` IS NOT the token's `miles.onboarding_required`.** That claim describes the identity store -
whether the SSO still needs a name before it considers the account known - and it is a boolean of the
**opposite polarity**. A user can be fully known to the SSO and still be `new_user` here. Reading one for the
other is how a sign-up gate ends up inverted.

Failure modes, and each wants different UI:

| HTTP | Body | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 401 | SSO's | Wrong or expired code. | Let them retype. |
| 429 | SSO's | Too many failures; the identifier is locked. | Show the lockout, do not retry. |
| 403 | `code: "account_blocked"` | Partner-imposed block. | **Terminal.** Show a permission message, not a login screen. Point at Miles support. |
| 403 | `code: "account_deactivated"` | Miles deactivation. | **Terminal.** Same, different team. |
| 502 | `{"message": "Sign-in could not be completed. Please request a new code."}` | Provisioning failed after a valid token. | **Retryable.** The code they used is spent - send them for a new one. |
| 503 | `{"message": "Sign-in is not configured on this environment."}` | Our configuration fault. | Not the user's problem. |

The two 403s are deliberately distinct: `active` and `is_blocked` are separate columns set by different people
for different reasons, and telling a blocked learner their account is "deactivated" sends them to the wrong
team. Neither carries a token or a cookie.

### 2.4 `POST auth-token-refresh/` - rotate the session

Serves both client shapes:

```json
{ "refreshToken": "..." }   // app clients
{}                          // web clients - the httpOnly cookie is forwarded upstream
```

`refreshToken` is optional for exactly that reason; requiring it would lock every browser out of refresh.

The same two local flags (`profile_status`, `is_test_user`) are merged into a 200 here, and **they matter more
on this route than on verify.**

**THE ONBOARDING SEQUENCE, which is the single most common integration bug on this surface:**

1. A first-time user verifies and comes back `profile_status: "new_user"`.
2. They complete the profile (section 4).
3. **You must refresh the token.** The claim is minted with the token, so skipping the refresh re-reads a stale
   value and bounces the user straight back into onboarding they just finished.

Two more rules:

- **Refresh before expiry, not after a 401.** The access token is deliberately short - it is the window in
  which a suspended user keeps access, and it cannot be revoked once issued.
- **Never run two refreshes concurrently.** Refresh tokens rotate and the old one dies about ten seconds after
  use, so parallel refreshes invalidate the caller's own session. Serialise them behind one in-flight request.

A `401` from this route (`"Session could not be refreshed. Please sign in again."`) means the refreshed token
would not resolve to a local row - the account is gone or deactivated. Send them to sign-in.

### 8.1 `faqs/` is public on purpose, and now says so

Its docstring used to claim "JWT required" while the code served anyone - it declared an authenticator but no
permission class, and **declaring an `authentication_classes` does not require authentication**: without a
permission class DRF falls back to `AllowAny`. The same defect was found and fixed on `questions/` on
2026-09-09.

Resolved on 2026-09-17 by making the intent explicit rather than by adding a token check: FAQs are help content
on a pre-login screen, and the maintainer's decision is that they stay open. The authenticator was removed
entirely, so a **stale or expired token can no longer 403 the FAQ list** - which is what would have happened
had the declaration simply been left in place beside an `AllowAny`.

`privacy-policy/` and `terms-and-conditions/` still carry the same missing permission class but compensate with
an explicit check in the handler, so they do refuse anonymous callers - with a 401 rather than a 403.

### 4.4 `PATCH profile/` - write them back

Query: `?form=onboarding` (default) or `?form=profile` - it names which milestone is in scope.

Body: the **same flat map** the GET returns, so you read, edit and send back without reshaping.

```json
{ "highest_qualification": "CA", "years_experience": 3 }
```

- **Partial by definition.** A code you omit is left exactly as it was, so a user can fill half a form, leave,
  and come back. This is why it is PATCH and not PUT.
- **`null` is refused**, not read as "clear". There is no clearing requirement yet and inventing one would fix
  that meaning forever.
- **Idempotent.** The same body twice yields the same rows and the same milestone. A retry after a mobile
  timeout is safe.

Response:

```json
{
  "answers": { },
  "profile_status": "onboard_completed",
  "is_onboarding_completed": true,
  "is_profile_completed": false,
  "missing": []
}
```

`answers` is the same flat map, nested rather than top-level because a bare map keyed by question code has
nowhere safe to carry metadata - a `profile_status` key would collide with a question coded `profile_status`.

**The write always succeeds; the milestone advances only when every required, shown question of that form has
an answer.** A partial save comes back with `missing` naming what is still outstanding rather than failing. Do
not treat a non-empty `missing` as an error.

A 400 is keyed by question code, one message per bad answer. Validation runs before the transaction opens, so a
rejected submission never partially applies.

**After this advances the milestone, refresh the token** - see 2.4.

### 4.2 `GET questions/` - what to render

Query: `?form=onboarding` (default) or `?form=profile`. An unrecognised value is a **400 naming the accepted
set**, never a silent fallback that would serve the wrong screen.

Response: `{"Questions": [...]}` - a **flat list** sorted by `display_order`, each question carrying its
`options`. `section` is a label you may group by; it does **not** affect ordering, and there are no screen
buckets. (Legacy keyed this by `Screen1` / `Screen2`. That is gone.)

A question whose `visibility` is `both` appears under **either** `form` value - that is why membership is one
column rather than two booleans.

**This route now requires authentication.** It did not before 2026-09-09: it declared an authentication class
but no permission class, which only *attempts* authentication, so it answered 200 to anyone. If you were
calling it pre-login, that no longer works.

## 3. `api/v1/account/user_details/` - the user record

JWT. `GET` and `PATCH`. **There is no user id in the path** - the row is always the caller's, so one client can
never address another's profile.

### 3.2 `PATCH` - 16 of those 28 are writable

```
first_name  middle_name  last_name  full_name  country_code
profile_picture  city  location  pathway  professional_qualification
work_experience  education  career_path  ai_readiness  learning_pathway
voluntary_enrollment_disclosure
```

Every field is optional; send only what changed. The response is the full GET projection.

**An empty body is a 400** (`"Send at least one field to update."`) rather than a 200 reporting a no-op.

The twelve withheld fields, and why, so you do not file these as bugs:

| Field | Why not writable |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `sso_user_id`, `created_at`, `updated_at` | System-owned. |
| `last_login` | Written by the auth path on a successful login. |
| `email`, `username` | SSO-owned. Changing an address is an identity-store concern. |
| `phone_number` | It is an OTP channel. Editing it here would let the number we message drift from the one the SSO authenticates. |
| `profile_status` | Advanced by whatever completes each step. Writable, a client could skip onboarding by setting one field. |
| `tags` | No documented owner, so not opened up on a guess. |
| `is_onboarding_completed`, `is_profile_completed` | Derived milestones. A client that could set them would skip onboarding. |

### 6.2 `GET web/app-status/` - JWT

```json
{
  "is_maintenance": false,
  "is_web_maintenance": false,
  "is_pathway": false,
  "is_onboarding_completed": true
}
```

| Key | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `is_maintenance` | Global mobile maintenance flag, **env only**. |
| `is_web_maintenance` | Web maintenance flag, env only. |
| `is_pathway` | Whether the user has selected a USP pathway. |
| `is_onboarding_completed` | Whether every always-asked onboarding field is filled. |

**`is_maintenance` honours the runtime override, and agrees with `app-maintainance/` GET.** Until 2026-09-17
it did not: it read the environment value directly while the other probe consulted the cache first, so an
operator who set an override put the mobile probe into maintenance and left this one reporting the app as fine.
Both now resolve the flag through one shared function, so the two cannot drift again. Either probe is
authoritative; they answer the same question the same way.

`is_web_maintenance` is env-only, and that is not the same gap: nothing writes a web override, so there is no
cache value for it to honour.

The two user-derived flags are cached per user for a short TTL; the two maintenance flags are read live on
every request, so a toggle is never masked by a warm entry.

## 3. `GET api/v1/events/register-via-zoom-status/<uuid:attempt_id>/`

The polling half of the handshake. Authenticated. Shared web + app. Takes NO query parameters - any query
string at all is a 400.

Scoped to the calling user, so one user cannot read another's attempt. A foreign or unknown id is
`404 attempt_not_found` rather than 403, which avoids confirming the id exists.

### 3.1 `200 OK`

```json
{
  "attempt_id": "9c2f1b70-8e4d-4a11-93cc-0d5a6f2e8b31",
  "status": "SUCCESS",
  "registration_status": "REGISTERED",
  "zoom_attempts": 1,
  "last_status_code": 201,
  "error_message": null,
  "error_code": null,
  "mf_retry_count": 0,
  "join_url": "https://us06web.zoom.us/w/8412...",
  "registered_email": "learner@example.com",
  "booking_id": "b41e77a2-1cf9-4c02-9c6e-3a8d5e0f1b22",
  "completed_at": "2026-09-17T09:14:22.118Z"
}
```

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `attempt_id` | UUID string | Echo of the path parameter. |
| `status` | string | The TEN-state internal status. Diagnostic, for Ops and support. Do not branch on it. |
| `registration_status` | string | The THREE-state client contract. Branch on this. |
| `zoom_attempts` | integer | How many times the Zoom leg has been tried. |
| `last_status_code` | integer or null | Last HTTP status seen from the external leg. |
| `error_message` | string or null | Human-readable reason. Safe to surface. |
| `error_code` | string or null | Machine-readable reason. |
| `mf_retry_count` | integer | Salesforce/MF forward retries. |
| `join_url` | string or null | The learner's own Zoom join URL. Populated once Zoom has issued it. |
| `registered_email` | string or null | The address this attempt actually sent to Zoom. On a FAILED attempt this is the only record of it, because the pipeline reads the profile live and the learner may have edited it since. This is the attendance-matching key. |
| `booking_id` | UUID string or null | Set once the `Booking` row exists. |
| `completed_at` | ISO-8601 string or null | Set when the attempt reached a terminal state. |

### 3.2 The three-state contract

`registration_status` is always one of:

| Value | Meaning | What the UI should do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PENDING` | Still working, or waiting on the Zoom host to approve the registrant. | Keep the spinner. Keep polling. |
| `REGISTERED` | The user IS registered on Zoom and holds a join URL. | Show the join affordance. Stop polling. |
| `REGISTER` | The pipeline stopped before a usable registration existed. | Show the retry CTA. Stop polling. |

The internal `status` collapses onto it like this:

| Internal `status` | `registration_status` |
| --- | --- |
| `SUCCESS` | `REGISTERED` |
| `MF_FAILED` | `REGISTERED` |
| `MF_PERMANENTLY_FAILED` | `REGISTERED` |
| `MF_SKIPPED` | `REGISTERED` |
| `ZOOM_FAILED` | `REGISTER` |
| `BOOKING_FAILED` | `REGISTER` |
| `INTERRUPTED` | `REGISTER` |
| `PENDING` | `PENDING` |
| `ZOOM_RETRYING` | `PENDING` |
| `ZOOM_PENDING_APPROVAL` | `PENDING` |

Two of these are worth understanding rather than just mapping:

- THE FOUR `MF_*` STATES ARE `REGISTERED`, not failures the user can act on. The Salesforce forward is an audit
  hand-off downstream of the fact that Zoom accepted the registrant. Telling the user to register again would
  be wrong AND would spend another Zoom registrant slot.
- `ZOOM_PENDING_APPROVAL` IS TERMINAL BUT MAPS TO `PENDING`. The Zoom host has to approve the registrant before
  a join URL is issued, and there is no action the user can take. A retry CTA there would invite a duplicate
  registration that Zoom answers with the same 409. The reason for the wait travels in `error_message` - show
  it. Note that polling this one will never resolve on its own timescale; see 4.2.

An unrecognised internal status collapses to `PENDING`, which is the safe default: a spinner rather than an
invitation to register twice.

### 3.3 Self-healing poll

If the worker handling an attempt died mid-pipeline (deploy, restart, crash), the row would otherwise sit
non-terminal forever and this endpoint would answer `PENDING` indefinitely - a spinner with nothing behind it.
Polling is exactly where that becomes observable, so it is where it is resolved: a stale attempt is reaped on
read and comes back as `INTERRUPTED` -> `REGISTER`, with

```
error_code: "stuck"
error_message: "The registration worker stopped before finishing (deploy, restart or crash).
                No Zoom registration was completed - please try again."
```

No cron has to have run for the client to get an actionable answer. Treat `REGISTER` as a genuine retry
affordance in this case - no Zoom registration was completed.

### 3.4 Refusals

| HTTP | `code` | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Any query parameter at all was sent. |
| 404 | `attempt_not_found` | No such attempt for this user. |

## 4. Driving the pair

### 4.1 The loop

1. `POST register-via-zoom/`.
2. `200` -> already registered, done. `202` -> take `attempt_id` and `status_url`.
3. Poll `status_url` until `registration_status` leaves `PENDING`.
4. `REGISTERED` -> show join, using `join_url`. `REGISTER` -> show retry, using `error_message`.

A sensible cadence is roughly every 2 seconds for the first 15 seconds, then back off. The happy path usually
resolves in a second or two; the pathological path is around 8 seconds of backoff.

### 4.2 Bound the poll

`ZOOM_PENDING_APPROVAL` is terminal but reads as `PENDING`, so a loop with no ceiling will spin on it forever.
Cap the poll (30-45 seconds is comfortable), and on timeout fall back to reading `status` and `error_message`
from the last response rather than continuing. That is the one place the internal `status` is worth reading on
the client, and it is for display, not for branching.

### 4.3 Do not re-POST to check state

A re-POST is safe - it will answer `200 already_registered` or `202` with the existing attempt - but it takes
the lock and writes a log line for nothing. Poll the status route.

## 2. `POST api/v1/events/register-via-zoom/`

Registers the authenticated caller for a webinar. Authenticated. Shared web + app.

This is a `202` handshake, not a synchronous registration. The endpoint answers immediately with an
`attempt_id`; the actual work - Zoom registrant, then `Booking` plus `BookingDetails`, then the Salesforce
forward - runs in the background. Poll the status route (section 3) for the outcome.

The reason is latency: the Zoom leg is three attempts with 1s and 3s backoff and the Salesforce leg is another
three, so a worst case that still ENDS IN SUCCESS is around six round trips and roughly 8 seconds. That is not
a request to hold open.

### 2.1 Request body

```json
{
  "webinar_id": "3f1a9c7e-5b42-4d9a-8f10-2c6be7d41a55"
}
```

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `webinar_id` | UUID | yes | The `Events.Webinar` PRIMARY KEY. Not the MF/SF integer id. |

ONE FIELD, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE BODY. Nothing else is accepted - see 1.3.

THE WEBINAR IS ADDRESSED BY UUID, which is a change from legacy. Legacy took the producing service's integer
and resolved it as `(webinar_id, webinar_type)` - a compound lookup, because that integer is unique only in
combination with the type. An integer-only lookup here would either need the type threaded through the client
contract or would silently resolve to whichever row Postgres returned first. Whatever feed hands you a webinar
should expose its `id`; `webinar-main-page` (section 6) does.

ONE INPUT SURFACE. Legacy read each parameter from the query string first and fell back to the JSON body. Here
the body is canonical - a query parameter on this route is a 400.

### 2.2 `202 Accepted` - the normal answer

```json
{
  "status": "accepted",
  "registration_status": "PENDING",
  "message": "Registration started. Pull to refresh.",
  "attempt_id": "9c2f1b70-8e4d-4a11-93cc-0d5a6f2e8b31",
  "status_url": "/api/v1/events/register-via-zoom-status/9c2f1b70-8e4d-4a11-93cc-0d5a6f2e8b31/"
}
```

`status_url` is built server-side off the URLconf, so it cannot drift from the real route. Prefer following it
over assembling the path yourself.

### 2.3 `200 OK` - already registered

Not an error. The caller already holds a live booking for this webinar, and NO pipeline is spawned.

```json
{
  "status": "already_registered",
  "code": "already_registered",
  "message": "You are already registered for this webinar.",
  "booking_id": "b41e77a2-1cf9-4c02-9c6e-3a8d5e0f1b22"
}
```

### 2.4 Idempotency, in two layers

The expensive mistake here is a duplicate Zoom registrant, so a double-tap is absorbed rather than refused:

1. A LIVE BOOKING -> `200 already_registered` (section 2.3).
2. AN IN-FLIGHT ATTEMPT (`PENDING` or `ZOOM_RETRYING`) -> `202` carrying THAT attempt's id, with
   `message: "Registration already in progress."` Poll the one already running; do not start a second.

A third guard sits under both: a short per-`(user, webinar)` lock. If two taps land inside the same few
milliseconds, the loser gets `409 registration_in_progress` with `retry_after_seconds`. Retry once after that
and you will get the in-flight `202`.

### 2.5 Every refusal

| HTTP | `code` | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Body failed validation, or carried an undeclared key. Carries `errors[]`. |
| 400 | `missing_email` | The user's profile has no email. Zoom requires one. |
| 400 | `invalid_email` | Profile email is malformed. |
| 400 | `missing_first_name` | Profile has no first name. |
| 400 | `invalid_first_name` | First name contains non-ASCII - in practice an emoji pasted into a profile. Zoom rejects it with a terminal 400. |
| 404 | `webinar_not_found` | No such webinar row. |
| 409 | `unsupported_webinar_type` | The row is not a `webinar` or an `offline` event. Orientations and premiers have their own flows. |
| 409 | `webinar_inactive` | Soft-deleted or temporarily deactivated. 409 AND NOT 404 DELIBERATELY - the row exists and your copy of it is not wrong, so do not discard the webinar; it may come back. |
| 409 | `webinar_cancelled` | The session was cancelled. A cancelled webinar stays `active=True`, so this is a separate flag rather than a variant of the one above. |
| 409 | `webinar_start_time_missing` | The webinar has no scheduled start time yet. An ops data problem, not a client error - surface `detail` and let the user retry later. |
| 409 | `registration_in_progress` | Lock contention. Carries `retry_after_seconds` (currently 15). Retry once. |

The four profile refusals are worth handling specifically: each `detail` is already written as user-facing copy
naming what to fix in the profile, and none is retryable without that fix. They are checked BEFORE any Zoom
call, so the user learns synchronously instead of polling to a terminal failure.

Order of evaluation, which is the order you will hit them: body validation -> webinar resolution (404 / the
four 409s) -> profile preflight (the four 400s) -> idempotency (200 / 202) -> lock contention (409).

### 2.6 `offline` webinars take the identical path

An in-person event still goes through the full Zoom -> Booking -> Salesforce write path, and the learner still
gets a Zoom registrant record and a join URL - they simply do not use it. No client branch is needed.

## 5. `GET app-api/v1/events/all-bookings/`

Every booking the calling user holds. Authenticated. App only; the web twin is not built.

**MOVED FROM `web-api/v1/events/all-bookings/` ON 2026-09-17.** Same view, same response, same route name
(`events-all-bookings-v1`) - only the prefix changed. There is no redirect.

`Booking` is one table serving two things under a database-level XOR: a row either points at a webinar or
carries a 1:1 `booking_type`, never both and never neither. This endpoint returns BOTH sides, each row tagged
with its `kind`.

### 5.1 Query parameters

| Param | Type | Default | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `window` | string | `all` | `all`, `upcoming`, `past` |

There is deliberately NO `kind` filter: both kinds come from one table in one query, so filtering server-side
would save no work, and you already receive them pre-bucketed.

Any other parameter is a 400.

### 5.2 Response

```json
{
  "message": "Bookings retrieved successfully.",
  "data": {
    "upcoming": { "webinar": [], "one_on_one": [] },
    "past": { "webinar": [], "one_on_one": [] }
  }
}
```

`data.upcoming` is present only when `window` is `all` or `upcoming`; `data.past` only when `window` is `all`
or `past`. Both inner keys are always present when their window is, empty rather than omitted.

THE SPLIT POINT IS NOW MINUS 30 MINUTES, not now. A session that is running right now still reads as
`upcoming` while the user is in it.

A booking with no start time is filed under `upcoming` and sorts to the top. That is not a bug: a booking we
cannot date is not yet KNOWN to be past, and it needs attention.

Cancelled bookings never appear on either side.

### 5.3 One row

  "kind": "webinar",
  "booking": {
    "id": "b41e77a2-1cf9-4c02-9c6e-3a8d5e0f1b22",

    "attended_status": "1",

    "total_poll_questions_available": 4,
    "total_webinar_duration": 3600,
    "attended_webinar_duration": 3240,
    "force_override_by_leadership_team": false
  },
  "details": {
    "id": "0f2b...",
    "book_id": "MF-99812",
    "datetime": "2026-09-20T13:00:00Z",
    "booking_url": "https://us06web.zoom.us/w/8412...",
    "registered_email": "learner@example.com",
    "spoc_name": null,
    "spoc_phone": null,
    "gmeet_link": null,
    "calendar_id": null
  },

| Key | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | UUID string | |
| `booking_type` | string or null | `null` on a webinar booking. One of `career` / `office` / `resume` / `alumni` on a 1:1. |

## 7. `GET web-api/v1/events/webinar-details-page/`

One webinar, in full - the page behind a card on `webinar-main-page`. **The surface follows your request**:
authenticated gets post-login, anonymous gets pre-login. There is no `login_type` parameter.

### 7.1 Query parameters

| `webinar_id` | uuid | yes | the `id` a main-page card carries |

There is deliberately no `login_type`, and sending one is a 400 (`extra_forbidden`) like any undeclared
parameter. `webinar-main-page` takes it because a signed-in visitor may legitimately want to preview the
signed-out page, so there the surface is a real choice. Here your token already answers it, and a parameter
that could contradict the token would be a second source of truth for one fact.

The id is the UUID, never `webinar_id_as_per_mf_sf` - that integer is unique only when paired with
`webinar_type`, and nothing in this backend hands it to a client.

### 7.2 Response

```json

  "data": { "login_type": "post_login", "webinar": { } }
}
```

produced by the same function, so the two screens cannot disagree.

`login_type` is echoed and is `pre_login` or `post_login`. It is more useful here than on the feed: there you
chose it, here it was DERIVED, so the echo is how you confirm which surface you got - and therefore whether
`registration` is present - without inspecting your own token.

### 7.3 The webinar object

**It is exactly the card object from section 8, plus four keys.** Render this page from the card type you
already have; the extras are additive. The shared keys are produced by the same function that shapes the
feed, so they cannot drift.

| --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | string \| null | The long-form page body; `short_description` is the one-liner. |
| `trailer_url` | string \| null | |
| `trailer_thumbnail_url` | string \| null | |
| `product` | object \| null | See below. Null as a whole when the webinar is tagged to no product. |

`product`:

| Key | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | UUID string |
| `name` | string |
| `mini_description` | string \| null |
| `description` | string \| null |
| `horizontal_image` | string (url, `""` when unset) |
| `vertical_image` | string (url, `""` when unset) |
| `square_image` | string (url, `""` when unset) |

`registration` (section 8.1) is present **only on an authenticated request**, exactly as on the feed. An
anonymous caller has no registration to report, so the key is absent rather than null.

`eligible` (section 8.2) is deliberately NOT emitted. It is a property of a BOOKING, the feed attaches it
only on `completed_webinar`, and computing it here would be a second definition of eligibility.

### 7.4 `product` and `subject` are two different columns and may disagree

Both name a row of `Masterclass.Subject`, reached by two different paths, and this endpoint reports both
rather than picking a winner:

- **`subject`** (a string, on the card) is the subject reached THROUGH `caira_masterclass_level`. The feed has
  emitted it since 2026-09-09 and it is untouched, so the two screens agree.
- **`product`** (an object, detail page only) is `Webinar.subject`, the direct FK, whose help text calls it
  "the Miles product this webinar is sold under" and says it SUPERSEDES the `caira_check` /
  `non_caira_check` pair.

They are independent columns, so a webinar tagged to a level of one subject and sold under another reports
both, honestly, under two names. **Which one wins is an open maintainer decision** - see section 9.8. Until
it is taken, prefer `product` where you need the commercial programme and `subject` where you need to match
what the feed showed.

### 7.5 Refusals

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | `webinar_id` missing, not a uuid, or any undeclared parameter |
| `403` | a bad or expired token. A request with NO token is served the pre-login surface, not refused |
| `404` | no webinar with that id is visible on this surface |

**The 404 is deliberately ambiguous.** "No such id" and "an id you may not see" are the same answer, so the
endpoint cannot be used to discover which ids exist. Visibility is the feed's own filter - soft-deleted,
cancelled, wrong login state and test webinars are all excluded before the id is matched, so a row the feed
hides cannot be opened by guessing.

Described in full in section 7.4. `Webinar.subject` (emitted as `product`) and

## 6. `GET web-api/v1/events/webinar-main-page/`

The webinar landing feed, in five buckets, for both sides of login. Web only.

This is a rudimentary first pass by request. The shape is the part that is settled; the bucket rules are
deliberately simple and each is a single filter, so a product correction is a one-line change.

### 6.1 Query parameters

| Param | Type | Required | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `login_type` | string | yes | `pre_login`, `post_login` |

DELIBERATELY REQUIRED, WITH NO DEFAULT. Defaulting to `pre_login` would mean a signed-in client that forgot the
parameter silently receives the anonymous page - a valid 200 that is wrong, with the two booking buckets empty
rather than absent. Omitting it is a 400 naming the parameter.

The vocabulary is `pre_login` / `post_login`, with underscores. Those two literals are the stored values in the
database columns this endpoint filters on, so there is one vocabulary end to end and no translation map.

### 6.2 Authentication is conditional

| `login_type` | Anonymous request | Request with a valid token | Request with a BAD token |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pre_login` | `200` | `200`, token resolved and ignored | `403` |
| `post_login` | `401 authentication_required` | `200` | `403` |

This is the only route in the app that is reachable anonymously and also serves per-user data. The branch
cannot live in a permission class - DRF resolves permissions during dispatch, before any view has read a query
parameter - so the view carries `AllowAny` and enforces the rule itself. It is a design, not a missing
`IsAuthenticated`.

A malformed or expired token is rejected on BOTH branches, including `pre_login`, rather than silently
downgraded to the anonymous page: a client sending a broken token has a problem it needs to see. That rejection
is the `403` from 1.2. The `401` here is the different case - a well-formed anonymous request asking for the
signed-in page - and it carries `message`, not `detail`:

```json
{
  "status": "error",
  "code": "authentication_required",
  "message": "login_type=post_login requires an authenticated request. Send a bearer token, or ask for login_type=pre_login."
}
```

### 6.3 Response

```json
{
  "message": "Webinar main page retrieved successfully.",
  "data": {
    "login_type": "post_login",
    "highlight_webinars": [],
    "upcoming_webinars": [],
    "completed_webinar": [],
    "absent_webinar": [],
    "missed_webinar": []
  }
}
```

EVERY KEY IS ALWAYS PRESENT, EMPTY RATHER THAN OMITTED. Fixed shape, varying contents - a rendering loop treats
an absent key and an empty list the same way, but a null check does not.

`pre_login` POPULATES THREE OF THE FIVE (amended 2026-09-18): `highlight_webinars`, `upcoming_webinars` and
`missed_webinar`. The two that stay empty are `completed_webinar` and `absent_webinar`, which are statements
about a BOOKING that an anonymous caller does not have. `post_login` populates all five, the three
backward-looking ones from the caller's own attendance.

The two plural keys and the three singular keys are inconsistent, and that is preserved deliberately: they
match the requested contract, and renaming a client contract to tidy it is a breaking change for cosmetic gain.

### 6.4 The five buckets

| Bucket | Per-user? | What is in it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `highlight_webinars` | no | Editorial. Driven by priority rows for THIS login state, lowest priority first. The absence of a row is the signal - an unranked webinar is not last, it is simply not here. Upcoming only. |
| `upcoming_webinars` | no | Everything visible in this login state that has not started, soonest first. |
| `completed_webinar` | yes | Past webinars the user ATTENDED. Each carries `eligible`. Post-login only. |
| `absent_webinar` | yes | Past webinars the user booked and did not attend. Post-login only. |
| `missed_webinar` | partly | Past webinars the caller is not committed to. BOTH login states - see below. |

`highlight_webinars` is a curated rail over the same webinars as `upcoming_webinars`, so the two lists overlap
by design. De-duplicate on `id` if your layout needs to.

Every bucket is capped at 20 rows. There is no pagination - this is a landing page, not a catalogue. The three
backward-looking buckets look back 90 days.

`absent` and `missed` are disjoint and the split is a product decision, not a schema fact: ABSENT is a live
booking the user did not honour, MISSED is a webinar they are not committed to.

THE ROUTING IS BY `attended_status`, AMENDED 2026-09-18. A booking the user CANCELLED now lands in
`missed_webinar`; it previously appeared in no bucket at all, so a cancelled webinar vanished from the page.

| `attended_status` | Bucket |
| --- | --- |
| `1` attended | `completed_webinar` |
| `2` not attended | `absent_webinar` |
| `3` registered | `absent_webinar` |
| `""` MF has not reported yet | `absent_webinar` |
| `4` cancelled | `missed_webinar` |
| no booking row at all | `missed_webinar` |

Cancellation reaches this endpoint on two independent columns - `status = false` (this system cancelled the
booking) and `attended_status = "4"` (MF reported it cancelled) - and BOTH route to `missed_webinar`, so the
same user action does not land in different buckets depending on which side recorded it.

ATTENDANCE OUTRANKS CANCELLATION. `attended_status = "1"` is `completed_webinar` even on a cancelled booking:
attendance is a fact about a session that already happened, a cancellation is a statement of intent about it,
and `completed_webinar` is the only bucket carrying `eligible` - so routing an attended row elsewhere would
withdraw the CPE / badge affordance from someone who earned it.

### 8.1 `registration` - on `highlight_webinars` and `upcoming_webinars`, `post_login` only

```json

  "status": "SUCCESS",
  "registration_status": "REGISTERED",

  "join_url": "https://us06web.zoom.us/w/8412...",
  "error_code": null,
  "error_message": null,

  "completed_at": "2026-09-17T09:14:22.118+00:00",
  "route_to_web_lms": false

```

Same three-state contract as section 3.2 - branch on `registration_status`, not on `status`.

The key is ABSENT on the `pre_login` branch (anonymous callers have no registration to report) and on the three
past buckets (registration is an affordance - register vs join - and a webinar that already happened offers
neither; `completed_webinar` answers the question those rows raise with `eligible` instead).

A user who registered before the attempt-row pipeline existed has a booking and no attempt. That case comes
back as `registration_status: "REGISTERED"` with `status`, `attempt_id`, `join_url` and `completed_at` all
`null` and `zoom_attempts: 0`. Do not read "no attempt id" as "not registered" - registering again would spend
another Zoom registrant slot on a seat they already hold.

`route_to_web_lms` is `true` only for an internal test user on a CAIRA webinar today. When `true`, open the
session in the web-LMS surface instead of `join_url`.

Boolean. `true` when the booking's `attended_status` is `"1"` (attended), or when leadership force-overrode it.

It is deliberately NOT recomputed from `attended_webinar_duration` against `total_webinar_duration`: the
thresholds live in the attendance ingest, and a second implementation of a rule that already exists elsewhere
is a rule that will disagree with itself.

### 9.1 `one_on_one` is always empty today

Reading 1:1 bookings works. Nothing in this repository CREATES one yet - the career-counselling write path is
not ported. So the `one_on_one` list is empty until that lands or historical rows are migrated in. An empty
list is not a fault. Build the card anyway; the shape is final.

Of the four `booking_type` values, only `career` can be newly booked. `office`, `resume` and `alumni` remain
legal to READ so historical rows keep resolving, so a reader must accept all four.

### 9.2 `webinar-main-page` does not filter by enrolment

`show_webinar_as_per_enrollment` (CPA / CMA / CAIRA / USP) is NOT applied, so the `post_login` upcoming list is
wider than a finished implementation's would be. Applying it needs the caller's enrolment set, which this pass
does not read.

### 9.6 No caching, no pagination on `webinar-main-page`

Every call hits Postgres, and the buckets are hard-capped rather than paginated. Expect that to change behind
the same response shape.
